nameStory: Johnston's balloon eolis gets its whimsical name from the balloon-like projections called cerata that cover its back, giving it a festive, inflated appearance. The name 'eolis' comes from Aeolus, the Greek god of wind, perhaps because these delicate sea slugs seem to dance through the water like they're carried by ocean breezes. Johnston likely refers to an early naturalist who first described or studied this species.
description: Johnston's balloon eolis is a tiny, translucent sea slug that looks like a living jewel crawling along the ocean floor. These delicate marine creatures are nudibranchs, which means 'naked gills' - they breathe through finger-like projections on their backs instead of having internal gills like fish. They're typically small enough to fit on your fingernail, with a soft, gelatinous body that can be nearly transparent to pale in color. As mollusks, they're related to snails and clams, but they've lost their shells entirely and developed their own unique beauty.

idTips.label: Balloon-like cerata
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature is the cluster of inflated, finger-like projections on the back that look like tiny balloons or clubs, often translucent and may contain colorful internal structures

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The body appears glassy or nearly transparent, allowing you to sometimes see internal organs through the skin, giving it an ethereal quality

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically very small, usually less than an inch long, requiring careful observation to spot among seaweed and rocks

idTips.label: Smooth, soft texture
idTips.description: The body feels like soft gelatin if gently touched, with no shell or hard parts anywhere on the animal

idTips.label: Two tentacles
idTips.description: Has a pair of horn-like tentacles (rhinophores) at the front of the head that help it smell and navigate underwater

habitat: Look for Johnston's balloon eolis in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and among seaweed beds at low tide. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found crawling on hydroids (small colonial animals) which they feed upon. You'll have the best luck finding them in protected coves and harbors where the water is relatively calm but still connected to the open ocean.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to warm, making this a good time to spot them moving among early-season marine growth in tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be seen feeding and reproducing, with warmer water making tide pool exploration more comfortable for observers.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall, though they may become less conspicuous as water temperatures begin to drop and marine activity slows.
seasonality.winter: Much harder to find as they retreat to deeper water or become less active, though dedicated tide poolers might still spot them on warmer winter days.

funFact: Johnston's balloon eolis can actually steal the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and store them in the tips of their balloon-like projections, essentially turning their prey's weapons into their own defense system - like a tiny underwater warrior collecting enemy ammunition!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small nudibranchs, but the distinctive balloon-like cerata set it apart from most relatives. Remember: if it looks like it's carrying tiny balloons on its back, you've likely found a Johnston's balloon eolis rather than other sea slugs with more pointed or branched projections.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Tergipes tergipes literally means 'back foot back foot' in Latin, referring to the way these animals seem to carry their breathing apparatus on their backs. Don't let the double name confuse you - this is a quirk of scientific naming where the genus and species names happen to be the same word.
compareHints: Since Johnston's balloon eolis is the only Tergipes species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other small aeolid nudibranchs in the region. Unlike many of its relatives that have pointed, finger-like cerata, this species has distinctly swollen, balloon-shaped projections that give it a more inflated appearance. The cerata are also typically fewer in number and more clustered than the numerous, scattered projections you'd see on many other sea slug species.
